x: The five BE behaviors: where they're taught, practiced, and labeled. How FYE 100 builds AI literacy: five observable behaviors, taught in the lessons, practiced in AI Chats, and labeled on every assignment. The course uses the BE framework, a student-facing, behavioral translation of the Digital Education Council (DEC) AI Literacy Framework used at the KCTCS system level. FYE 100 covers Tier 1 (Benchmark), which maps to DEC Level 1. The framing question across the course: How do students make intentional decisions about using AI while maintaining ownership of their learning? No Mile Marker requires AI. The AI Chats are the course's graded AI practice, done in Blackboard's AI Conversation tool. Every behavior is framed around judgment, including the decision not to use AI. The five BE behaviors All five are introduced in Lesson 1.3 and Lesson 1.4 . Be Safe and Be Honest are baseline expectations from Module 1 on. Be Critical, Be Responsible, and Be Reflective recur as course anchors. Behavior What it means at Tier 1 DEC dimension: Level 1 BE Safe Recognize AI-generated content and understand basic risks of sharing personal or sensitive information with AI tools. Understanding AI and Data: AI and Data Awareness BE Honest Disclose AI use when required; understand the difference between AI assistance and your own work. Ethical and Responsible Use: Understand Risks BE Critical Evaluate AI output: verify information, identify bias, and assess accuracy before using it. Critical Thinking and Judgement: Question AI Output BE Responsible Make intentional decisions about when and how to use AI to support your learning, not replace your thinking. Ethical and Responsible Use: Understand Risks BE Reflective Notice how AI use affects your learning process and growth. Human-Centricity, EI, and Creativity: Awareness of Human-AI Interaction DEC Dimension 5, Domain Expertise, is intentionally out of scope for FYE 100. It belongs to Tier 2 program courses.

Blackboard AI Chats Four modules include an AI Chat with Coach Pathfinder in Blackboard. The chats in Modules 2, 8, and 9 are Socratic: Coach Pathfinder asks questions instead of giving answers, so the thinking stays with the student. The Module 4 chat is a role-play: the student works through a scenario with Coach Pathfinder and does the evaluation themselves. If a student has a concern about the AI Chats Students are told to talk with their instructor if they have a concern about using the AI Chats, such as an accommodation, a privacy objection, or discomfort with AI. Each AI Chat has a backup journal in Blackboard for this. Any student who would rather not use AI can ask for it. The journal covers the same learning without AI, and it's released one student at a time, on request, so the chat stays the default for everyone else. Keep the journal hidden. Don't open it to the whole class. Release it to that student only. Set the journal's visibility to Release conditions, choose Specific members, and pick the student. Grade the journal the same way as the chat: half for answering its parts, half for the closing reflection. The chat itself is half for finishing the conversation and half for the closing reflection. Enter that score in the AI Chat column. The journal doesn't count toward the course grade, so the score only counts once you type it into the student's cell in the AI Chat's gradebook column. A hidden note with these steps sits next to each backup journal in Blackboard. AI Chats are course communication Students are told, in the syllabus, the AI Chat Trail Tip, and each chat's instructions, that the chats are part of the course and that you read every conversation. The same community standards apply as in email and discussions. Coach Pathfinder is set up to name that expectation once, calmly, and keep coaching. Casual frustration, like a mild swear word in passing, isn't a conduct issue. Let it go. Language aimed at Coach Pathfinder (cursing at it, insults, slurs, sexual or threatening content) gets a private message from you. Treat it as a professionalism conversation, not a punishment. Many students don't think of the chat as part of class. If it looks like resistance to using AI at all, offer the alternate journal. Score the chat on the usual criteria. Don't deduct for language. If the student never actually worked through the conversation, the "finish the conversation" half isn't earned, the same as any unfinished chat. Threats, harassment, or anything that suggests a student may be unsafe: handle it the way you would in any class, under the KCTCS Code of Student Conduct and OCTC's reporting procedures. x: The appreciative mindset Appreciative Advising starts with a habit of attention: look first for what is working. When a student is struggling, it is natural to go straight to the problem and hand over a fix. The appreciative approach begins with the student's strengths and uses them to work on the problem. Here is the difference in three situations you will meet in FYE 100: Deficit-focused "You've missed two Mile Markers. What happened?" Appreciative "You turned in four Mile Markers on time. What was working those weeks? Let's use that for the two that are missing." Deficit-focused "This STAR(T) story is too vague." Appreciative "The part where you called your Success Coach is the strongest moment here. Tell me more about what you did next." Deficit-focused "You need to go to tutoring." Appreciative "What has helped you in a class like this before? Here's who can help with that, and here's how to reach them." Appreciative does not mean easy. The model ends with a phase called Don't Settle, and it asks for high expectations all the way through. You are still naming what is missing. You start from what the student has already shown they can do. Where it comes from Jennifer Bloom, Bryant Hutson, and Ye He introduced the six-phase model in The Appreciative Advising Revolution (2008). It draws on Appreciative Inquiry, positive psychology, and social constructivism.

x: The six phases The phases run in order, and they also loop. A student who reaches Don't Settle sets a higher goal, and the cycle starts again. The six phases, read clockwise from the top. Model: Bloom, Hutson, and He (2008). Disarm. Make a warm first impression so students feel safe. Discover. Ask open questions to learn students' strengths and stories. Dream. Invite students to share their hopes for the future. Design. Build a plan together to reach those hopes. Deliver. Students carry out the plan, with your support. Don't Settle. Challenge students, and yourself, to raise the bar.

x: The course as a six-phase journey Each phase below says what it is for, what students are doing during that stretch of the course, and what you can do to help. The "Try saying" lines are examples to adapt for an announcement, a comment on a Mile Marker, or a conversation after class. 1 Disarm Modules 1 and 2 Put students at ease so they are open to learning. Many arrive expecting college to be intimidating, and first impressions form fast. What students are doing Getting oriented, naming why they are here in Mile Marker #1, mapping a support team, meeting their Success Coach, and practicing how to ask for help ( Modules 1 and 2 ). Your part Welcome students by name in your first announcement and your first replies. Answer early messages quickly and warmly. The first reply sets the tone for the term. Share a little of your own first-term story when it fits. Treat asking for help as a normal thing capable students do. Try saying "I'm glad you're in this section. What would make this a good term for you?" 2 Discover Modules 3, 4, 5, and 7 Learn who the student is and what they already do well. Positive, open-ended questions bring out strengths, skills, and stories. What students are doing Finding out where their time and energy go ( Module 3 ), how they study ( Module 4 ), where their money goes ( Module 5 ), and what their strengths and values are ( Module 7 ). The Appreciative Advising Inventory, given in Module 5, belongs here too. Your part Ask open questions in your feedback, and follow up on the answers. Name the strengths you see in what students report, especially ones they did not name themselves. When a student describes a rough patch, ask what they learned from it. That retelling is the groundwork for STAR(T) Stories. Try saying "Your time log shows you studied every morning before work. What made that stick?" 3 Dream Module 8 Invite students to say what they hope for, in their career and their life, and take the answer seriously. What students are doing Researching one career in depth, testing it for fit against their strengths and values, and asking what future that career would make possible ( Module 8 ). Your part Respond to the dream before you respond to the obstacles. Connect it to what the student discovered earlier: their strengths, values, and interests. When something does not line up, raise it as a question the student can explore. Try saying "You said helping people one-on-one is one of your top values. Where does that show up in the career you researched?" 4 Design Modules 6 and 9 Work with the student to build a plan that turns the dream into steps. The goal is to teach students how to plan and decide, so they can do it again without you. What students are doing Drafting an academic plan and writing questions for their Success Coach ( Module 6 ), then learning the 4C Check and drafting a first STAR(T) story ( Module 9 ). Your part Plan with students. Ask what they would choose and why before you offer an answer. Break big goals into small next steps. Watch your vocabulary. "Credit hour," "prerequisite," and "AAS" are new words to many first-term students. Make referrals specific: a person, a place, and what to ask for. Try saying "Which part of this plan are you least sure about? Let's figure out who can answer that." 5 Deliver Modules 10, 11, and 12 Students carry out the plan. Your confidence in them matters, and so does being honest that there will be obstacles and more than one way around them. What students are doing Finishing their Merit activities and naming how they work with others ( Module 10 ), taking a first step in a community they belong to and choosing their three stories ( Module 11 ), then telling those stories in the capstone ( Module 12 ). Your part Say plainly that you believe the student can do it, and say why. Follow up on what students said they would do. Remind students that a setback means trying another route. End the course the way you started it: warmly, and by name. Try saying "You chose your three stories last week. Which one are you most ready to tell, and what's in the way of the others?" 6 Don't Settle Module 12, and all term Keep raising the bar. Support and challenge go together: recognize what the student did well, then ask for more. What students are doing Looking back at their Starting Point, comparing their two Skills Snapshots, writing the Transfer step of each STAR(T) story, and planning how to finish the rest of the term ( Module 12 ). Your part Praise the specific action, then ask for the next level. Use this phase in feedback all term. It is where "good enough" becomes "your best." Hold the same standard for yourself. The model asks instructors to keep improving too. Try saying "This answer is solid. What would make it one you'd be proud to say out loud in an interview?"

x: Virtual meet-ups Merit asks students to attend three activities. Students who are on campus during the day can walk into an event. Online and commuting students mostly choose on-demand options, which they can finish from anywhere, but alone. A virtual meet-up is the one Merit option that works from anywhere and still puts students with other people. It is Disarm and Discover in practice: students meet you and each other, and you learn who they are. Taking part is up to you. There are two ways to do it, and the first one costs you nothing. Tier 1 Announce the shared sessions Each term, a small number of virtual sessions are open to every FYE 100 student, whatever their section. They are run by whoever has a session ready. A Life Design Workshop is one example. The Dean of Student Success maintains the calendar. Your part. Announce the sessions to your students, and remind them as each one comes up. Why it works. One instructor can't offer evening, midday, and weekend times. A shared calendar can, and that is what lets a student who works evenings finish Merit. Have an idea for a session? Contact the Dean of Student Success to propose it. Tier 2 Host your own If you'd like to host a meet-up for your own section, 30 minutes is enough. You don't need approval. Instructors have discretion over what counts for Merit, so a meet-up you host counts. Welcome and introductions, about 5 minutes. Have everyone share their name and one thing about their week. One topic, about 15 minutes. Pick something students are dealing with right now. See Topics that work . Open questions, about 10 minutes. Let students ask you, and each other, whatever is on their minds. Use Microsoft Teams. FYE 100 courses connect to Teams through Microsoft Education, so you can create the meeting inside your course. Students join from the course, with no separate link or login. Merit proof A meet-up counts as a virtual activity, so students attach proof instead of signing a roster. Tell students to take a screenshot of the meeting window during the session. Proving attendance afterward is much harder. If you need to confirm who attended, Teams can give you an attendance report. Topics that work The Merit reflection asks students what they attended, what they learned or now think about differently, and how it connects to their goals. A session that covers only logistics gives students little to say about the last two. Choose a topic students can think about: What to do when a plan stops working How to decide whether to withdraw from a course What this term has taught you so far Taking stock of what you've already finished In a series of sessions, include at least one on taking stock. Students are good at coming up with options, but many don't feel they are making progress. Looking at what they have already done helps. Make it worth showing up for. A session that sounds useful or fun draws more students than one that sounds like a requirement.

s: Why FYE 100 grades the way it does
l: Instructor Guide · Grading and Late Work
x: Why FYE 100 grades the way it does FYE 100 is where students practice being college students: planning ahead, asking for help, following through, and recovering when a plan falls apart. Most will make their first college mistake somewhere. This course is the best place for it, because here the mistake costs little and the recovery teaches a lot. That makes FYE 100 different from a course like ENG 101, where polish, mechanics, and precision are part of what's assessed. Here we assess whether a student can show a habit or a skill in their own life. Grade the evidence of that, not the quality of the writing around it. Think of your role as an instructor who coaches. You set clear expectations, assess the work, and help the student see a next step. The student decides what they can commit to and follows through. A coaching question can be as simple as "What's one assignment you can finish this week, and when will you work on it?"

s: What every section shares, and what's up to you
l: Instructor Guide · Grading and Late Work
x: What every section shares, and what's up to you A few things are the same in every section, so students earn the same grade for the same work no matter whose section they're in: the rubrics for Mile Markers and STAR(T) Stories what earns credit, below the catch-up window for late work Everything else is your call: how you give feedback, how you run class, what you accept outside the window, and what extra flexibility you offer a student with a plan. Your experience and judgment are part of what makes the course work.

l: Instructor Guide · Grading and Late Work
x: What earns credit Start with the assignment criteria and look for what the student actually shows you. They may tell a story out of order, or use an example from home that seems ordinary at first. If the evidence is there, count it. Full credit: the work shows what the assignment asks for. A short, specific response can do that. Partial credit: some of the learning is there, and a required piece is missing or too general. Give credit for what's there and name the piece to work on. No credit: nothing was submitted, or nothing in it relates to the task. If the work is still open, tell the student what they can do next. We don't deduct for grammar, spelling, length, or formatting unless the assignment asks for them. A student who answers every prompt honestly in plain language has done the work. Example. A STAR(T) Story describes stepping in as center during a tied game and helping the team win, then ends with "It's important to adapt." Situation, Task, Action, and Result are there; the Transfer doesn't name where the skill comes next. That story earns credit for four of the five steps. A coaching response: "You knew the playbook cold, and it paid off when the team needed you. Where off the field might someone need you to step in like that, and how will you be ready?"

l: Instructor Guide · Grading and Late Work
x: Grading Mile Markers Every Mile Marker uses the same rubric, attached to each Mile Marker assignment in Blackboard. It counts answered prompts. An answer counts when it responds to the prompt and is about the student, with at least one real detail from their own life, results, or work. It doesn't have to be insightful, polished, or long. How deep an answer goes belongs in your feedback, not the score. Level What it means Complete Every prompt is answered. One Missing One prompt is missing or blank. About Half About half the prompts are answered. Minimal Only one or two are answered. No Response Nothing submitted, or nothing relates to the prompts. When you grade Use the "A strong answer" note as the standard. Each prompt's note says what specific looks like for that prompt. Grade to the note, not to your own idea of a strong answer. Don't deduct for length, grammar or spelling, writing style, a simple example, an honest answer the prompt allows (such as "I didn't use AI this week"), or a conclusion you'd disagree with. Between two levels, choose the higher one. Name the prompt for anything that didn't count. For example: "Prompt 2: this could apply to anyone. What's one action that fits your week?" If you can't point to a prompt, the credit stays. Coaching to the scale early In the first few Mile Markers, leave a one-line comment on full-credit work too, naming what made it specific. Students learn the scale faster from what earned credit than from what didn't. Point students to How Mile Markers are scored in How to Use This Book. It explains full credit in student language, with a short example of general versus specific. If your section's scores run noticeably higher or lower than others, compare a few submissions with another instructor. A short norming conversation closes most gaps. Revise and resubmit Every Mile Marker allows two attempts, and the last attempt is the one graded. Whether to invite a revision is your call. Consider offering it, especially early in the semester. A student who rewrites a general answer into a specific one has learned the scale. If you invite a revision, name the prompt to revise and what would make it specific. Then grade the new attempt. If a student resubmits on their own, grade the new attempt. Blackboard counts the last graded attempt, so the first grade stays until you grade the new one.

l: Instructor Guide · Grading and Late Work
x: Scoring STAR(T) Stories Each of the three stories is scored the same way, whether it's recorded or written: credit for each STAR(T) step the student completes. A step counts when it's there and it's about the student. The rubric is attached to each submission portal in Blackboard. Step It counts when it... Situation Sets the scene: where, when, and what was going on. Task Says what the student needed to do or solve. Action Says what the student did, not only what "we" did. Result Says what happened because of what they did. Transfer Names where they'll use this skill next. A response that isn't a true story about the student, or doesn't use STAR(T), earns no credit. Recorded stories are never scored on delivery, only on the story and its structure. Transfer is the step most often missed. "This will help me in my future career" doesn't name a place. The fillable forms and the practice guides break Transfer into three prompts: what the story showed, where the student will need the skill next, and what they'll do when they get there. Point students to those prompts in your feedback.

x: Scoring AI Chats Each AI Chat is scored the same way: half for finishing the conversation, half for the reflection. Each chat's instructions name what "finished" means, such as an observation for every SIFT move and a verdict in Module 4, or a response for each C and a next step in Module 9. Either it's in the transcript or it isn't. Grade the reflection like any other response. It counts when it's specific and about the student. "It was helpful and made me think" doesn't. Length isn't scored. The chats are course communication. Students are told you read every conversation, and the same community standards apply as in email and discussions. Don't deduct for language. If a student's language is aimed at Coach Pathfinder, send a private note and treat it as a professionalism conversation. If cursing or arguing took the place of the conversation, the "finish" half isn't earned, the same as any unfinished chat. Each chat allows two attempts, and the last attempt is the one graded, the same as the Mile Markers. Whether to invite a second try is your call. Any student who would rather not use AI can ask for the alternate journal. It's scored the same way, half for its parts and half for the closing reflection. Whether a student who already did the chat can switch to the journal is your call. The full guidance, including what to do about threats or a student who may be unsafe, is in Blackboard AI Chats .

x: Late work and recovery Weekly due dates set the pace, and we encourage students to meet them so they can use feedback as the course moves along. Deadlines are real. Recovery is real too, and the student starts it. Most individual work stays open until a catch-up date. Students can submit before then without asking permission, and late work is graded on the usual criteria, so it can earn full credit. The syllabus tells students the same thing. Work Last day to submit (11:59 PM Central) Modules 1 to 7 The Tuesday after Spring Break Modules 8 to 11 The Tuesday after Module 11 is due, the next day Module 12 and the STAR(T) Stories Their posted Sunday deadline. No catch-up date. The exact dates are on each semester's course calendar and in the hidden instructor notes in Modules 7 and 10. Why the dates fall where they do Tuesday cutoffs. Students are used to Monday due dates, so the window closes the day after, and nobody finishing Monday-night work gets shut out. Spring Break. Break falls between Modules 8 and 9, so the first window closes the Tuesday after it. Students who are behind can use break to catch up; students who are caught up don't have to do anything. Module 8 is due Monday as usual, the first day of break, so it belongs to the second window. Students who want a work-free break finish it early. Grading time. Final grades are due within 48 hours of the course ending. The second cutoff leaves about a week to grade the last batch. What the window covers Covered: individual work, including Mile Markers, AI Chats, tasks, the BE Check, journals, the Skills Snapshots, and Merit reflections. Discussions (online): a late initial post can still earn credit for the post. Replies to classmates can't be made up once the discussion has moved on. Attendance (in person) can't be made up. Merit Activities are part of the window, but keep nudging students toward the module dates: the activity listings thin out late in the semester. Anything else, or any work after a catch-up date, is your call. Closing a window Hide the modules in that window after 11:59 PM on the cutoff date. The next morning works. Hide the module, never the items in it. Students see a "not available" note, and their grades and feedback stay visible. Hiding a graded item also hides its grade. The readings stay open in the guidebook. To reopen work for one student, add a release condition to the closed module for that student. Reopen when there's a realistic plan to finish and you have time to grade it. Any extension still ends with Module 12, unless the student has an IP grade.

l: Instructor Guide · Grading and Late Work
x: The gradebook The master shell's gradebook is set up so students can see where they actually stand. Keep these settings in your section. The overall grade shows points: points earned out of points possible. Two more columns show the same standing in other formats: YOUR CURRENT LETTER GRADE and YOUR CURRENT GRADE PERCENTAGE. Keep "Assign automatic zeroes" turned on. Missing work becomes a zero once its due date passes. Without it, the overall grade counts only the work that's been graded, so a student with six missing assignments can see a B and believe they're doing better than they are. What a student sees in Student Preview: the overall grade in points at the top right, then the letter grade and percentage as the first two rows. On your side of the gradebook, the two extra columns look like ordinary calculated columns, so check the student view after any change. Automatic zeroes and the catch-up window work together. A zero isn't final while the work is still open. When a student submits during the catch-up window, grade it, and the score replaces the zero. Say this to students early, so a zero reads as "missing, and I can still fix it," not "too late."

l: Instructor Guide · Grading and Late Work
x: IP (in-progress) grades When extenuating circumstances keep a student from finishing by the end of the 12 weeks, you can assign an IP grade instead of a final grade. An IP gives that student time past the end of the course to finish. It's for circumstances the catch-up window can't cover, not a replacement for it. The student asks. You can tell a student that an IP is an option, but the request comes from them. Meet to make a plan. Meet with the student (virtual is fine) and agree on which assignments are left, a date for each, and how they'll submit. Spread the dates out so the work gets done over time, not all at the end, and set email check-ins as needed. We recommend all IP work be due by noon on the Friday of finals week. Send a short written summary so you both have the same list, and make sure the student knows unfinished work earns no credit. Enter IP as the final grade, and leave the course open. Don't select Mark as Completed until the student's work is done and graded. Marking it complete closes the course to students. Reopen what the student needs with a release condition on each closed module. Submit a grade change form by the Monday after finals week. The IP changes to wherever the student's grade stands: an E, or a C or B if they finished some of the work but not all of it. Then mark the course as completed.

x: Coaching a student who falls behind Make the first step easy to see. A student who's overwhelmed may need help choosing where to start: "If you're wondering where to start, start with your Professionalism story. Coaching notes Where students tend to get stuck this module, and what helps. Two very different starting points share the room. Recent high school graduates (including dual-credit students as young as 16) and adults returning after years away often sit side by side. Lesson 1.1 speaks to both on purpose. Naming both out loud on day one tells returning adults their work experience counts, and tells younger students the support is there if they go looking. "I didn't know" usually means "I didn't read the syllabus." Expect questions this week that the syllabus already answers. Point students back to it kindly and specifically ("It's under Late Work on page 3"). That's the habit Lesson 1.1 is building. Mile Marker #1, Question 4: goals that are too vague. "Do better" and "pass" are the common weak goals. Use the book's test: could someone else tell whether you reached it, and could you put each step on a calendar? Students reuse this goal later in the course, so it's worth a quick nudge now. Question 5: every stance on AI is a fair answer. Some students are excited about AI, some are skeptical, and some would rather not use it at all. The question asks for a clear position, not a positive one. Make that explicit, especially for students who expect the course to push AI. The BE Check is practice for the vocabulary. Students match the five BE behaviors from Lesson 1.3 to real situations. If several students miss the same item, clear up that behavior in your next announcement or class. The same five behaviors come back all semester. Blackboard basics trip up more students than the content. Finding the module, submitting a file, and reading feedback are new to many students. The optional Syllabus and Blackboard Scavenger Hunt is low-stakes practice; encourage anyone who seems lost to try it before Mile Marker #1 is due. Ask for profile photos early. A photo in Blackboard (Lesson 1.5) makes discussions and feedback feel personal for everyone, you included. A short reminder in week 1 gets most students to do it.

Active learning ideas Pick one or two. Each fits in a 50-minute class alongside the slides. Before and now Time: 10 minutes You need: The four Before / Now shifts from Lesson 1.1, on the screen Students silently pick the shift that will take the most adjustment for them. They move to a corner of the room assigned to that shift (or raise a hand for each one). Each group names one thing they'll do this week to get ahead of it, and shares it with the room. Why it works: Turns Lesson 1.1's reflection question into a visible, low-risk conversation, and students see they aren't the only ones. Online sections: Post the four shifts as a poll or quick survey, and share the results in your next announcement. Syllabus speed hunt Time: 10 minutes You need: The FYE 100 syllabus (or another course's syllabus) open on devices In pairs, students race to find five things: a due date, the late work policy, how to contact you, the AI Course Policy, and one thing that surprised them. First pair with all five shares where they found each one. Close by asking which item they'd have missed if they'd only skimmed. Why it works: Practices the "syllabus is a contract" habit with the real document, not a description of it. Online sections: Point students to the optional Syllabus and Blackboard Scavenger Hunt in Blackboard, which does the same job. Name that tune Time: 5 minutes You need: Your voice Hum the bassline from Lesson 1.3 and ask the room what song it is. Let both answers come out, then ask: was anyone wrong? Connect it to AI: it completes the most likely pattern, which isn't always the right answer. Introduce the word hallucination. Why it works: A memorable, low-tech way into pattern completion. Students remember the song long after they forget a definition. Online sections: Tell the story in your recorded mini-lecture; it works just as well on video.

Introducing a partner, instead of yourself, lowers the stakes on day one. Facilitating: Model it first with your own answer. Listen for strengths students name in passing (work ethic, caring for family, a trade skill) and point them out: those are the answers to Mile Marker #1, Question 3.

Coaching notes Where students tend to get stuck this module, and what helps. Students need to read the source document before the AI Chat. Is This Legit? is a role-play built on a source document that lives in Blackboard. Students who skip it flounder in the chat. Put "read first" in your announcement, and use the instructor key in Blackboard when you review the chats. Question 1: "I studied more" isn't a strategy. Look for a named strategy and how the student used it. The four from Lesson 4.2 (retrieval practice, spaced practice, asking why, and interleaving) give students words for what they tried. Question 2 rewards honesty over success. A strategy that didn't work, explained honestly, is a strong answer. Say so in your feedback; students often assume they have to report that everything went well. SMART goals drift back to vague. Question 3 is where "study more" reappears. Ask: could someone else tell whether you did it, and when? A goal like "Quiz myself for 15 minutes after each biology class, starting this week" is the target. Question 4 is about honesty, not where AI use landed. Full credit doesn't depend on staying at brainstorming. It depends on an honest account of where AI use landed and whether that was intentional.
